newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OLYMPICS-MANDELA HAILS CAPE TOWN 2004 SHORTLISTING.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-MANDELA HAILS CAPE TOWN 2004 SHORTLISTING.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela on Friday hailed Cape Town's inclusion in a shortlist of cities bidding to host the Olympic Games in 2004 as a boost for the African continent.

"The prospect of an Olympic Games in Cape Town presents South Africa with yet another challenge to play an active role in the African renaissance," he said in a statement after Cape Town was named as one of five finalists for the Games.

Thousands of black and white South Africans waited in Cape Town's Waterfront tourist area with crossed fingers held aloft as the International Olympic Committee (IOC) announced the finalists in Lausanne, Switzerland.
Men, women and children leaped to their feet, hugged, danced and cheered as Cape Town's name was read out in a live radio broadcast from Lausanne.

Five girls released white doves, and thousands of balloons in the colours of the South African flag were released over the harbour. Fog prevented a planned victory flypast by a jetliner painted in the colours of the flag.
The IOC's selection committee named Athens, Buenos Aires, Cape Town, Rome and Stockholm from among 11 candidates after studying a detailed technical report of each bid.
Istanbul, Lille, Rio de Janeiro, San Juan, Seville and St Petersburg failed to make the cut.
Local officials welcomed the decision but warned there was a long way to go before Cape Town could hope to reap the economic benefits of being the first African Olympic venue.
"From now we are going to redouble our efforts to win the Games," said provincial sports minister Lerumo Kalako.
Nomaindia Mfeketo, head of the city's executive committee, warned that administrators would have to convince the city's impoverished black majority that the event would be worth the financial risk.
"There are challenges facing us and one of them is to show our communities the truth of what we said about this bid being a developmental tool," she said.
"We need to interact and work together, not only as the public and private sectors but with the community."
Phillip Krawitz, president of the South African Chamber of Business, said success in September, when the Games will be awarded, could catapult South Africa into the world economy.
"For Cape Town, it's an incredible opportunity. For South Africa, it's an unbelievable opportunity. For Africa it's the beginning of our renaissance.
"The Olympics unleashes the most powerful economic force on earth. Business sees this as an opportunity to build this city, this country and this continent," he said.

Krawitz said the Games could boost gross domestic product by up to two percent and generate up to 30 billion rand ($6.7 billion) between 1997 and 2006. As many as 100,000 permanent jobs could be created.
Ngconde Balfour, a senior member of Cape Town's Olympic Bid Committee and former black activist, was confident the city would now go all the way and win the race to stage the Games.
"I knew deep down in my heart, I knew," he said. "In September we will win, and in 2004, we will present the most unique, the most magnificent, the most wonderful African Games."
Balfour said Cape Town's bid was unique because it cast the Games as a central plank of social reconstruction after centuries of white rule.
"The Olympics is not a prize, it is a tool to make sure that we transform this country," he said.
South African business has already contributed about 70 million rand to the bid campaign but support has fallen below the initial expectations of the bid managers.
Cape tourism chief Gordon Oliver said on Friday, however, the IOC's vote of confidence should release millions more from the private sector.
"The business community already recognises the need to provide the kind of funding we have never seen before," said Oliver.
"We have to spend money but spend it well and wisely and assertively to really do an outstanding job."
